prompt.context: After successfully servicing large beverage companies over the last 20 years, our client, the CEO of High Quality Bottles (HQB), a small plastics manufacturing and bottling company, wants to expand into the hospitality and leisure space. Specifically, she wants HQB to supply local hotel chains with bottled toiletries like shampoos, conditioners, body wash, and lotions. HQB already has the interest of local hotels in their hometown.
prompt.question: How would you approach finding the market size for the first year in this expansion?

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the city?
clarifying_info.a: Medium sized city, about the size of Seattle or Dallas

clarifying_info.q: How many hotels are in the local market?
clarifying_info.a: There are roughly 50 hotels in the region

clarifying_info.q: Are we looking for dollar value or units?
clarifying_info.a: The client is primarily focused on market size in dollar value

clarifying_info.q: What is the goal / what makes this a desirable venture?
clarifying_info.a: Right now the client only wants to know market size, but later profitability — namely potential profit margins above 25% — will be important in determining if the market is attractive

clarifying_info.q: How broad of a market is HQB looking at?
clarifying_info.a: The client's only focus is the local hotel market

clarifying_info.q: Which products is HQB looking to supply?
clarifying_info.a: Only shampoos, body wash, conditioners, and lotions for each hotel room — 1 bottle each for a total of 4 per hotel room

clarifying_info.q: How big is HQB's business currently?
clarifying_info.a: HQB currently does $20 million in revenue

exhibits.title: Regional Hotel Industry Statistics
exhibits.shows: Key statistics about the regional hotel market including number of hotels, rooms per hotel, occupancy rate, and room turnover frequency

data.note_bottles_per_stay: HQB estimates the average guest will use 2.5 bottles per stay
data.note_stays: The average stay is two nights, which means each room typically turns over 3 times a week

framework: Room Count: number of hotels in region × average rooms per hotel = total rooms
Occupancy: average occupancy rate and average length of stay (or room turnover per week)
Order & Replenishment: number of bottles per room (initial stock), average bottles used per stay (replenishment), and price charged per bottle
Year 1 market size = initial order value + replenishment order value over 50–52 weeks

questions.prompt: What is the market size of supplying hotel toiletries in this region in dollars in Year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate two components: (1) the initial stocking order for all hotel rooms, and (2) ongoing replenishment throughout the year. Strong candidates recognize both components are needed for Year 1. The price per bottle ($0.50) is not on the exhibit and must be asked for.

math.setup: Initial order: total rooms × 4 bottles/room. Replenishment: occupied rooms per week × 2.5 bottles/stay × stays/week × weeks/year. Price = $0.50/bottle.
steps: Initial order bottles: 6,000 rooms × 4 bottles = 24,000 bottles
math.answer: Year 1 market size ≈ $912,000 (using 50 weeks) or ~$948,000 (using 52 weeks). Both are acceptable; rounding to 50 weeks is encouraged.

questions.prompt: What profit margin can HQB expect in Year 1 if it captured 100% of the market?
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify all cost components and apply straight-line depreciation (not full CapEx). Key insight: only Year 1 depreciation ($25,000) is used, not the full $250,000 CapEx. Raw material + ingredient cost is $0.25/bottle (50% of $0.50 revenue). Distribution cost is $0.05/bottle ($1.00/case ÷ 20 bottles). Fixed labor is $100,000/year. Answer in range 25–30% is acceptable.

math.setup: Revenue − Fixed Labor − Variable Material Costs − Distribution Costs − Depreciation = Profit; Profit ÷ Revenue = Profit Margin

questions.prompt: Considering that HQB's average profit margin on its beverage operations is 25%, is this new business opportunity attractive?
questions.guidance: Generally yes — the new hospitality business yields slightly higher margins (26–27%) than the existing beverage business (25%). Candidate should tie the quantitative result back to the client's stated threshold and offer a clear recommendation.

brainstorming.prompt: What other information should the client know to determine whether this is an attractive business to enter into?

categories.name: Internal Factors
ideas: Cost of plastics and raw materials
Factory capacity — can existing capacity handle new volume?

categories.name: External Factors
ideas: Number of competitors and competitive intensity in the local market
Health of local tourism economy (leisure travel demand)
Health of local business activity (business travel demand)
Emergence of threats to hotels such as Airbnb reducing hotel stays
Sustainability trends — recycling, water usage, plastic reduction regulations

recommendation: HQB should pursue the expansion into supplying hotel toiletries in the local market
The Year 1 market size is approximately $912k–$948k; at 100% capture, profit margins of ~26–27% exceed HQB's 25% beverage benchmark
risks: Fluctuations in raw material and ingredient costs could compress margins below the 25% threshold
Single-region concentration creates geographic risk if local hotel demand declines
Realistic market share will be below 100%, reducing absolute profit dollars
next_steps: Evaluate scale expansion beyond the local region to grow addressable market
Explore input cost hedging strategies to protect margins against raw material volatility
Conduct competitive analysis to size realistic market share capture
